title: 10. Security & Auth: CSRF (Cross-Site Request Forgery)

sections.title: Explanation
sections.body:
> **In one line:** CSRF (Cross-Site Request Forgery) is an attack where a malicious website tricks a victim's browser into making an authenticated request to a target site where the victim is already logged in, causing the target site to perform an action as the victim without the victim's knowledge or consent.

CSRF exploits a fundamental property of the browser: it automatically attaches credentials (cookies, HTTP auth, client TLS certificates) to every request it makes to a given origin, regardless of which site initiated the request. If you are logged into `bank.com` (so your browser holds a `bank.com` session cookie), and then you visit `evil.com` which contains a hidden form that POSTs to `bank.com/transfer`, your browser will send the request along with your session cookie — and `bank.com`, seeing a valid session, will execute the transfer. The attacker never sees the cookie (same-origin policy protects the response), but they don't need to: they just need the action to happen. This is why CSRF is sometimes called a "one-click attack" or "session riding" — the attacker rides the victim's existing session. The attack is silent: there is no prompt, no visible navigation, and the victim may not realize anything happened until they check their account balance.

The historical damage is substantial. In 2008, an Indiana University researcher published details of a CSRF vulnerability in YouTube that allowed an attacker to add videos to a victim's "Favorites" list, send messages as the victim, and add the attacker to the victim's friend list — all without the victim's knowledge. Netflix had a CSRF hole in 2006 that let an attacker change a victim's shipping address and reorder DVDs. ING Bank had a CSRF flaw that allowed fund transfers. Twitter, YouTube, and Meta have all had CSRF-related bugs over the years. The cumulative lesson is that any state-changing endpoint protected only by a session cookie is vulnerable, and CSRF was for years one of the most common and damaging web vulnerabilities — OWASP listed it in the Top 10 from the very first list in 2003 through 2013, when it was retired (incorrectly, many argue) because mitigations became standard. CSRF still appears in modern applications, particularly in less-mature frameworks, internal admin interfaces, and APIs that accept cookie-based auth without CSRF protection.

The core mitigation is the **CSRF token** — a cryptographically random value that the server generates, embeds in every form (typically as a hidden input) or returns in a response header, and validates on every state-changing request. The token must be unguessable (32+ bytes of CSPRNG output), tied to the user's session, and present in the request for the action to succeed. The key insight is that the attacker's site cannot read the token (same-origin policy blocks the attacker's JavaScript from reading the response of a `GET` to the target site), so they cannot include it in their forged POST. Django, Rails, Flask, Express, and Spring Boot all ship CSRF middleware that does this automatically — Django's `{% csrf_token %}` template tag and Rails' `protect_from_forgery` are the canonical examples. The token can be **synchronizer token pattern** (server stores the token in the session and compares) or **double-submit cookie** (token is stored in a cookie and in a header, server compares the two; the attacker can't set both because they can't write to the target's cookie domain). The double-submit pattern is stateless and scales better, but requires careful cookie handling.

Beyond tokens, modern defense is layered. **SameSite cookies** (introduced in Chrome 51, 2016) let the server mark a cookie as `SameSite=Lax` (sent only with top-level navigations from the same site, not with cross-site POSTs) or `SameSite=Strict` (sent only with same-site requests, period). `SameSite=Lax` defeats the classic CSRF POST attack while preserving the "click a link to log in" UX; `SameSite=Strict` is more secure but breaks the "follow a link from an email to your dashboard" UX because the cookie is not sent and the user appears logged-out. Chrome's 2020 default of `SameSite=Lax` for cookies without an explicit `SameSite` attribute eliminated a large class of CSRF attacks across the web overnight. **Custom headers** (like `X-Requested-With` for AJAX, or `X-CSRF-Token`) provide defense because cross-site requests cannot set arbitrary custom headers without CORS preflight — so a request with a custom header is, by construction, a same-origin request or a CORS-approved cross-origin request. **Origin and Referer headers** let the server verify the request came from the same site; if `Origin` is missing or unexpected, reject the state change. The strongest defense combines several of these: SameSite=Lax cookies + synchronizer token + Origin header check.

The trade-off is security versus friction and compatibility. `SameSite=Strict` breaks SSO redirects (when the IdP redirects back to the SP, the SP's cookies aren't sent) and email-link flows; some third-party integrations require `SameSite=None; Secure` cookies, which re-enable the CSRF attack surface. CSRF tokens add a small per-request validation cost (a session lookup or HMAC comparison) and require careful handling in single-page apps where forms are rendered client-side — the token must be fetched from the API or embedded in the initial HTML. Stateless JWTs stored in `localStorage` (not cookies) are immune to CSRF by construction (the browser does not auto-attach them), but they introduce XSS-based token theft risk — moving the problem from CSRF to XSS. For stateless JWT-in-cookie architectures (more secure against XSS), the token must be paired with CSRF protection again. The right answer is usually: keep session/auth in an `HttpOnly`, `SameSite=Lax` (or `Strict`) cookie, pair it with a synchronizer or double-submit CSRF token, validate the `Origin` header, and require a custom header for state-changing AJAX. Layer the defenses so that no single failure breaks the system.

Finally, CSRF applies only to cookie-based (or other auto-attached) authentication. APIs that use `Authorization: Bearer <token>` headers (where the browser does not auto-attach the token) are immune — the attacker cannot read the token from `localStorage` due to same-origin policy, and they cannot forge a header. This is why CORS exists: to relax the same-origin policy safely for cross-origin API calls. The modern API pattern (mobile apps and SPAs using bearer tokens) has shifted the threat landscape from CSRF toward XSS and token theft. But cookie-based web apps — the majority of internet traffic — remain vulnerable, and CSRF protection must be standard. A 2024 web app that ships without SameSite cookies and CSRF tokens is shipping with a known, preventable, decade-old vulnerability class.

POST /transfer->| Cookie: session=abc | | | body: to=attacker&amt=1000 | | | [target sees valid session, | | | executes transfer!] | |<---- 200 OK -------| (SOP blocks attacker reading) | | | Victim loses $1000 silently. DEFENSE LAYERS (any one stops the attack; layer them): +-------------+ +-------------+ +-------------+ +-------------+ | SameSite | | CSRF Token | | Origin hdr | | Custom hdr | | =Lax/Strict | | (sync/dbl) | | check | | (X-CSRF) | +------+------+ +------+------+ +------+------+ +------+------+ | | | | v v v v cookie not sent token mismatch origin != bank no X-CSRF header on cross-site -> 403 -> 403 -> 403 POST (attacker can't (evil.com is not (cross-site can't read token) same-origin) set custom hdr) ``` ### Walkthrough 1. The victim logs in to `bank.com` normally; the server sets a session cookie (HttpOnly, but no SameSite attribute — the historical default). The browser stores it and will attach it to every future request to `bank.com`, regardless of which site initiated the request. 2. The victim, in the same browser session, visits `evil.com` (perhaps by clicking a link in a phishing email or following a link from a compromised site). The evil server returns an HTML page containing a hidden auto-submitting form whose `action` points to `bank.com/transfer` with attacker-controlled fields. 3. The browser renders the evil page and auto-submits the form via `POST` to `bank.com/transfer`. Because the request targets `bank.com`, the browser attaches the `bank.com` session cookie — the attacker never sees the cookie itself (same-origin policy blocks the response), but the cookie rides along. 4. `bank.com` receives the POST with a valid session cookie, has no CSRF protection, assumes the request came from the victim (it's "their" session), and executes the transfer. The response is sent back, but the same-origin policy prevents `evil.com`'s JavaScript from reading it — the attacker doesn't need the response, just the side-effect. 5. To prevent this, the server should issue a CSRF token (random 32+ bytes) on the session, embed it as a hidden input in every form, and validate it on every state-changing POST. The attacker's site cannot read the token (SOP blocks reading cross-origin responses), so they cannot include it in their forged form, and the server rejects. 6. Additional layers: set `SameSite=Lax` on the session cookie (browser will not send it on cross-site POSTs), check the `Origin` header on state-changing requests (reject if `Origin` is not the expected site), and require a custom header like `X-CSRF-Token` on AJAX calls (cross-site cannot set custom headers without CORS preflight). Layering means a single failure does not break the system.

sections.title: Code
sections.body:
**What this code covers**

- Synchronizer-token + HMAC double-submit cookie generator/validator.
- Issue a fresh CSRF token + double-submit cookie for a session.
- Validate a state-changing request.
- Rotate the token (after login, after privilege change).
- CSRF token generator + validator (synchronizer + double-submit hybrid).
- Demonstrates the two main patterns: server-stored sync token and
- Stateless double-submit cookie (HMAC-bound to session id).
- Secret is the per-application HMAC key (rotate via KMS)

```python
# CSRF token generator + validator (synchronizer + double-submit hybrid).
# Demonstrates the two main patterns: server-stored sync token and
# stateless double-submit cookie (HMAC-bound to session id).
import os, hmac, hashlib, time, secrets

class CSRFProtection:
    """Synchronizer-token + HMAC double-submit cookie generator/validator."""

    def __init__(self, secret: bytes):
        # secret is the per-application HMAC key (rotate via KMS)
        if len(secret) < 32:
            raise ValueError("secret must be >= 32 bytes")
        self.secret = secret
        self._session_tokens = {}  # session_id -> {token, expires_at}

    def issue(self, session_id: str, ttl: int = 3600) -> dict:
        """Issue a fresh CSRF token + double-submit cookie for a session."""
        token = secrets.token_urlsafe(32)  # 256 bits of entropy
        expires_at = time.time() + ttl
        self._session_tokens[session_id] = {
            "token": token, "expires_at": expires_at,
        }
        # Double-submit cookie: HMAC(session_id || token) bound to session.
        mac = hmac.new(self.secret, f"{session_id}:{token}".encode(),
                       hashlib.sha256).hexdigest()
        return {
            # Server-rendered form field (synchronizer token)
            "form_field": f'<input type="hidden" name="csrf_token" '
                          f'value="{token}">',
            "token": token,
            # Set-Cookie value: bearer of the double-submit proof
            "cookie_value": f"{token}.{mac}",
            "cookie_attrs": "Path=/; Secure; SameSite=Lax; HttpOnly=False",
            "expires_at": expires_at,
        }

    def validate(self, session_id: str, header_token: str,
                 cookie_value: str, origin: str, expected_origin: str,
                 method: str) -> bool:
        """Validate a state-changing request. Returns True only if all
        checks pass: token matches session, cookie HMAC matches, Origin
        header is the expected site, and method is state-changing."""
        # 1. Method check: only state-changing methods need CSRF protection
        if method not in ("POST", "PUT", "PATCH", "DELETE"):
            return True  # GET/HEAD/OPTIONS are safe (should be read-only)

        # 2. Origin header check (defense in depth)
        if origin and origin != expected_origin:
            return False

        # 3. Session token lookup (synchronizer pattern)
        record = self._session_tokens.get(session_id)
        if not record:
            return False
        if time.time() > record["expires_at"]:
            del self._session_tokens[session_id]
            return False
        # Constant-time comparison to prevent timing attacks
        if not hmac.compare_digest(record["token"], header_token):
            return False

        # 4. Double-submit cookie HMAC verification (catches stolen tokens
        #    that weren't paired with the right cookie)
        try:
            tok_part, mac_part = cookie_value.split(".", 1)
        except ValueError:
            return False
        expected_mac = hmac.new(self.secret,
                                f"{session_id}:{tok_part}".encode(),
                                hashlib.sha256).hexdigest()
        if not hmac.compare_digest(expected_mac, mac_part):
            return False
        if not hmac.compare_digest(tok_part, header_token):
            return False
        return True

    def rotate(self, session_id: str) -> dict:
        """Rotate the token (after login, after privilege change)."""
        self._session_tokens.pop(session_id, None)
        return self.issue(session_id)

# --- Demonstration ---
if __name__ == "__main__":
    csrf = CSRFProtection(secret=os.urandom(32))
    session_id = "user_session_42"
    creds = csrf.issue(session_id)
    print("Issued token:", creds["token"][:16] + "...")

    # Legitimate request from same-origin with all protections in place
    ok = csrf.validate(
        session_id=session_id,
        header_token=creds["token"],
        cookie_value=creds["cookie_value"],
        origin="https://bank.com",
        expected_origin="https://bank.com",
        method="POST",
    )
    print("Legitimate POST accepted:", ok)  # True

    # CSRF attack: attacker has no token, no cookie, wrong Origin
    blocked = csrf.validate(
        session_id=session_id,
        header_token="",  # attacker cannot read real token
        cookie_value="",
        origin="https://evil.com",
        expected_origin="https://bank.com",
        method="POST",
    )
    print("CSRF attack blocked:", not blocked)  # True
```
